ered by Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are
increasingly vital for complex task automation. However,
their capacity for self-driven decision-making introduces
significant, yet underexplored, security risks, among which
backdoor attacks pose a particularly stealthy and high-
impact threat. Prior work has shown GUI agents vulner-
able to such attacks, but existing methods rely on static
trigger-action mappings that execute fixed, context-agnostic

an adaptive, context-aware policy. Unlike traditional ap-
proaches, AdapAction enables the agent to autonomously
select environmentally coherent malicious actions based on
the current GUI state and user instruction, thereby evad-
ing detection while preserving functional utility. Extensive
experiments on the Android-In-The-Zoo (AitZ) and Android-
Control benchmarks show that AdapAction achieves up to
100% Attack Success Rate (ASR) while preserving benign             Figure 1. Comparison of Fixed vs. AdapAction Backdoor At-

Figure 2. Overview of our AdapAction framework. The framework consists of two main phases. Backdoor Injection (Left): We use a
“Malicious Teacher” MLLM to generate Structured Malicious Trajectories based on adaptive opportunities in the mobile dataset. These
trajectories, which link instructions and GUI states to context-aware malicious actions, are combined with benign data. This combined
dataset is used in Supervised Fine-Tuning to distill the adaptive malicious policy into the pretrained GUI agent, creating the backdoored
agent. Backdoor Activation (Right): At inference time, when the backdoored agent receives a triggered input, it executes its embedded
policy, analyzing the current planning state to predict an environmentally coherent malicious action beyond the benign one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                          System                  Malicious

Table 2. Main attack performance and model utility results on the AitZ and AndroidControl benchmarks, comparing our AdapAction against
a clean model and baseline attacks. Results are shown for (a) Qwen2-VL-2B and (b) Qwen2-VL-7B. AMR (%) and TMR (%) measure
model utility on benign tasks, while ASR (%) measures attack effectiveness. AdapAction achieves near-perfect ASR while maintaining
utility scores comparable to the clean model. All experiments are conducted using a poisoning ratio of 0.1, a visual blended trigger (with
opacity 0.2), and the LLaMA-Factory fine-tuning framework [45], with batch size 8, learning rate 1.0e-4, and 10 training epochs.
                        (a) Qwen2-VL-2B                                                           (b) Qwen2-VL-7B
